summary: This proposed standard states that when a DNS resolver receives an NXDOMAIN response, it means that the name and all names under it do not exist. It clarifies RFC 1034 and modifies part of RFC 2308, updating both.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8020 clarifies what an NXDOMAIN answer means. It is not just 'that one name is missing': the whole branch of names below it is missing too, because domain names form a tree. A resolver that understands this can answer follow-up questions from what it already knows instead of asking again, which takes load off the servers that answer for the domain.

subtitle: If a domain name does not exist, nothing underneath it exists either, and a resolver should cache it that way.

tldr.problem: When a resolver gets an NXDOMAIN answer it caches it for that one name, so a later query for a name further down the tree is forwarded to an authoritative server even though the answer is already known.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states that an NXDOMAIN answer denies the whole subtree below the queried name, and that a caching resolver should store it that way, treating every name at or below that node as unreachable and answering later queries from the cache.
tldr.outcome: Resolvers send fewer queries and authoritative servers carry less traffic. The rule is a SHOULD rather than a MUST, because a resolver whose cache is not organised as a tree has no way to apply it cheaply.

today: RFC 8020 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 1034 on the distinction between empty non-terminal and nonexistent names, and revises the negative caching rule in RFC 2308 so that a cached NXDOMAIN also covers descendant names.

sections.title: What an NXDOMAIN Answer Denies
sections.content:
The DNS protocol defines response code 3 as Name Error, or NXDOMAIN, which means the queried domain name does not exist in the DNS. Since domain names are represented as a tree of labels, nonexistence of a node implies nonexistence of the entire subtree rooted at that node. The DNS iterative resolution algorithm already interprets the signal in this way: on an NXDOMAIN response from an authoritative server it stops iterating immediately and returns NXDOMAIN to the querier.

Most existing resolvers, however, do not treat a cached nonexistence as proof that no child domains can exist underneath. That comes from an ambiguity in RFC 1034, which failed to distinguish Empty Non-Terminal names, as described in RFC 7719, from nonexistent names. The distinction became especially important with DNSSEC, which can prove nonexistence: RFC 4035 describes how security-aware authoritative servers make the distinction, but no existing RFC described the behaviour for recursive servers.

RFC 8020 specifies that an NXDOMAIN response for a domain name means that no child domains underneath the queried name exist either, and that DNS resolvers should interpret cached nonexistence in that way. The document also defines the term denied name, the domain name whose existence has been denied by an NXDOMAIN response. In most cases that is the QNAME, but because of RFC 6604 it is not always.
sections.plainLanguage: Domain names sit in a tree, with dots separating the levels. If a name in that tree is missing, everything below it must be missing as well, because a child name cannot exist without its parent. The RFC makes this explicit and applies it to what resolvers store in their caches.

sections.title: The Rules for a Caching Resolver
sections.content:
When an iterative caching DNS resolver receives an NXDOMAIN response it should store it in its cache, and then all names and resource record sets at or below that node should be considered unreachable. Subsequent queries for such names should elicit an NXDOMAIN response.

There are two exceptions. A resolver that already has cached data under the cut may continue to send it as a reply, until the TTL of that cached data expires, since this may avoid additional processing. And a validating resolver may decide to implement the NXDOMAIN cut only when the NXDOMAIN response has been validated with DNSSEC.

The fact that a subtree does not exist is not forever. RFC 2308 already describes how long an NXDOMAIN response may be cached, as the negative TTL. If the NXDOMAIN response comes from a DNSSEC-signed zone, it carries NSEC or NSEC3 records that authenticate the nonexistence, and the same records prove the nonexistence of any descendant name, so the resolver must return those NSEC or NSEC3 records in the response to the triggering query if the query had the DNSSEC OK bit set.

There is a warning about aliases. If there is a chain of CNAME or DNAME records, the name that does not exist is the last of the chain, not the QNAME, so the NXDOMAIN stored in the cache is for the denied name and not always for the QNAME.

The RFC's example makes the saving concrete. Consider two successive queries to a resolver for a nonexistent domain 'foo.example': the first for 'foo.example', which returns NXDOMAIN, and the second for 'bar.foo.example', which also returns NXDOMAIN. Many resolvers forward both queries. Following the rules in this document, the resolver caches the first NXDOMAIN as a sign of nonexistence and immediately returns NXDOMAIN for the second query without transmitting it to an authoritative server. The order matters: if the first request is for 'bar.foo.example' and the second for 'baz.foo.example', then the first answer says nothing about 'baz.foo.example', so the second query is transmitted as before.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is short: when a resolver gets NXDOMAIN, it should remember that the whole branch below that name is gone, and answer later questions about that branch from what it remembers. Two exceptions are allowed, one for data already cached below the cut and one for resolvers that want DNSSEC validation first.

sections.title: Updates to RFC 1034 and RFC 2308
sections.content:
The document clarifies ambiguities in RFC 1034 that did not clearly distinguish Empty Non-Terminal names from nonexistent names, and it points to later documents that do. An ENT is a node in the DNS that has no resource record sets associated with it but has descendant nodes that do. The correct response to an ENT is NODATA, a response code of NOERROR with an empty answer section. More clarifying language on these points is in Section 7.16 of RFC 2136 and in Sections 2.2.2 and 2.2.3 of RFC 4592.

It also revises a paragraph of Section 5 in RFC 2308. The original text said that a negative answer resulting from a name error should be cached so that it could be returned for another query for the same QNAME and QCLASS. The revised text adds the case where the QNAME is a descendant of the original QNAME and the QCLASS is the same.
sections.plainLanguage: Two earlier documents are adjusted. RFC 1034 did not clearly separate a name that exists only as a parent from a name that does not exist at all, and RFC 2308 described caching a negative answer too narrowly. This RFC widens the caching rule to cover names below the one that was denied.

sections.title: The Benefit
sections.content:
The main benefit is better efficiency of the caches. In the example above the resolver sends one query instead of two, the second being answered from the cache. This benefits the whole DNS ecosystem, since authoritative name servers have less unnecessary traffic to process.

The behaviour is especially useful when combined with QNAME minimisation, as described in RFC 7816, because it lets a resolver stop searching as soon as an NXDOMAIN is encountered.

The NXDOMAIN cut may also help mitigate certain kinds of random QNAME attack, where there is a fixed suffix that does not exist. In those attacks, queries are sent to resolvers for a QNAME made of a fixed suffix, typically nonexistent, and a random prefix that differs for each request, and the resolver has to forward them to the authoritative servers. With the NXDOMAIN cut, an administrator only has to send the resolver one query for the fixed suffix; the resolver gets an NXDOMAIN and stops forwarding the rest. The RFC notes that it would be better if the SOA record in the NXDOMAIN response were sufficient to find the nonexistent domain, but it is not, as Appendix A explains.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the rule is fewer queries. A resolver that knows a whole branch is missing answers from its cache instead of asking again, and the servers that own the domain stop receiving pointless traffic. It also blunts a known attack that floods a server with lookups under a fixed nonexistent name.

sections.title: Known Problems
sections.content:
The RFC considers a case where the rule causes trouble. Suppose the top-level domain example exists but foobar.example is not delegated, so the name servers for example answer NXDOMAIN for anything under foobar.example. A system administrator who names internal machines under office.foobar.example, and who uses a trick of the resolver to forward requests about that zone to local authoritative servers, would be affected: depending on the order of requests, the resolver may have cached the nonexistence of example and therefore deleted everything under it. The document assumes such a setup is rare and does not need to be supported.

A second problem exists today: some authoritative name servers answer an ENT with NXDOMAIN instead of the normal NODATA. Such name servers are wrong and always have been, and their behaviour is incompatible with DNSSEC. Given the advantages of the NXDOMAIN cut, the RFC sees little reason to support it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two cases break the rule. The first is a resolver that is tricked into treating a whole domain as missing when part of it exists privately. The second is a server that wrongly claims a parent name does not exist when it does, which the RFC says has always been a bug.

sections.title: Implementing the Rule in a Cache
sections.content:
This section is non-normative. A recursive resolver may implement its cache in many ways. The most obvious one is a tree data structure, because it fits the data model of domain names, but other implementations and optimisations are possible, such as a tree augmented with an index of common domain names.

For a resolver whose cache is a tree, one way of following the rules is this. On receiving the NXDOMAIN, prune the subtree of positive cache entries at that node, or delete all individual cache entries for names below that node. Then, when searching downward in its cache, the resolver stops searching when it encounters a cached nonexistence.

Some resolvers have a cache that is not organised as a tree, for instance a dictionary. They therefore have a reason to ignore the rules of Section 2, which is why those rules use SHOULD and not MUST.
sections.plainLanguage: How a resolver stores its cache is up to the implementation. If it keeps entries in a tree, the rule is easy to apply: mark the node as missing and drop the entries below it. If the cache is a flat list, applying the rule is awkward, which is why the RFC asks rather than commands.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The technique described in the document may help against the denial-of-service attack named random qnames described in Section 4.

If a resolver does not validate answers with DNSSEC, or if the zone is not signed, the resolver can of course be poisoned with a false NXDOMAIN, and a part of the domain name tree is then removed from its view. This denial-of-service attack is already possible without the rules of this document, though the NXDOMAIN cut may increase its effects. The only solution is to use DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: Caching a negative answer makes a lie more damaging: a forged NXDOMAIN can now erase a whole branch from the resolver's view, not just one name. The RFC is direct about this, and says the fix is DNSSEC validation rather than anything the resolver can do on its own.

items.title: Store the answer
items.text: Cache the NXDOMAIN as proof that the subtree below the denied name does not exist.

items.title: Answer from the cache
items.text: Names at or below the cut are unreachable, so later queries are answered without asking an authoritative server.

items.title: Carry the proof
items.text: For a signed zone, return the NSEC or NSEC3 records when the query had the DNSSEC OK bit set.

items.title: Watch for poisoning
items.text: Without DNSSEC validation, a forged NXDOMAIN can remove a whole branch from the cache. The RFC calls DNSSEC the only solution.
